MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
## The route: B, then A, then C

This is the only order that works:
- **A can't come first.** Unloading at A can't start before 09:00, which means arriving at B at 09:40, after the shop opens at 09:30.
- **C can't come before A.** C won't accept anything before 11:00, by which time A's window has closed.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B, unload |
| 09:05 | Leave B (done 25 min before opening) |
| 09:30 | Arrive at A, unload (window 09:00–10:00) |
| 09:45 | Leave A |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** |
| 11:00 | Unload at C |
| 11:15 | Leave C |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** |

**This plan has no slack at the end.** C can't start unloading until 11:00, and the drive back takes 45 minutes, so 12:00 is the earliest possible return whatever else happens. If C keeps the driver waiting, or the unload runs over, he'll be late.

Earlier in the day there are only about 5 spare minutes after the break, plus 15 minutes of leeway at B.

If 12:00 is a hard deadline, it's worth either:
- asking C whether they'd accept delivery from 10:45, or
- telling whoever needs the van back that it may be a few minutes late.

## Van name ideas

- **Chester** (as in chest of drawers)
- **Dovetail**
- **Van Gogh**
- **Polly Sh** (a French-polishing pun)

## Friendlier "driver arriving" text

> "Hi [name], our driver is on his way and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!"

## Evening-before text, under 160 characters

> "Hi Sam, your furniture from Oakleaf Restorations is due tomorrow between 9:00 and 10:00. Any problems, just reply to this text. Thanks!"

With that example name and company it's **135 characters**. The fixed wording is about 103 characters, which leaves around 50 for the name, company and times.

Use straight apostrophes and no emoji. Curly quotes or emoji switch the message to a different encoding with a 70-character limit per part, so it would be split or charged as several messages.

## Three checks before handover

1. **Condition.** Check the whole piece for new scratches, chips, dents or marks to the finish, ideally against photos taken at loading.
2. **Moving parts.** Open and close every door and drawer, and check that hinges, handles, locks and castors work.
3. **Complete and stable.** Make sure all parts, keys, shelves and fixings are there, the protective wrapping is off, and the piece stands level without wobbling.

Have the customer look at the piece with the driver before signing.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Email**, with the customer signing on the driver's phone at handover. It's quicker, it can't get lost, and it gives you a timestamped record. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer them.

## Proof of delivery, for the part-timer

> "Proof of delivery is the record showing that an item was delivered and accepted, usually the customer's signature and name, with the date, time and a photo of the item in place."
